content: The administration of baloxavir was implemented as a single upfront dose. Consequently, all patients managed under the PCR-treat strategy received a complete course of treatment, comparable to the Treat all strategy. Both strategies were associated with a loss in quality-adjusted life days (QALDs) when compared to the Treat none strategy, primarily due to the higher incidence of adverse events. The appropriateness of treatment was evaluated by examining the proportion of patients with non-severe influenza-like illness who were appropriately treated and the proportion of patients without influenza who were inappropriately treated. In the visual representation, green bars indicated influenza patients who received treatment, striped green bars represented patients without influenza who did not receive treatment, red bars denoted untreated influenza patients, and red-striped bars showed patients without influenza who received treatment. In 2022, the World Health Organization (WHO) published guidelines for the clinical management of severe illness caused by influenza virus infections. The development of these guidelines began in 2016 but was delayed due to the COVID-19 pandemic. Given that the previous guidelines were initiated over seven years earlier and did not address non-severe influenza, the WHO guideline steering committee identified the need for an updated guideline. Planning for this update began in late 2022, and gaps in the previous guidelines were identified. In May 2023, a planning document was submitted to the WHO Guidelines Review Committee for approval. After two additional revisions, it was approved in January 2024. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) was composed of a multidisciplinary team, including technical experts in influenza, researchers, frontline clinicians, patient representatives, and other stakeholders. For this update, the GDG also included an expert in health ethics, equity, and justice to address the challenges of providing recommendations that consider varying global access to influenza therapeutics and diagnostics. WHO ensured gender balance and representation from all WHO regions within the GDG. The initial GDG meeting was held on October 2, 2023. During this meeting, it was confirmed that the updated guideline would build upon the 2022 guideline, incorporating recommendations for the treatment of non-severe disease and the use of antivirals as prophylaxis for influenza. PICO (Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcome) questions were formulated to guide the evidence review. The population of interest included individuals with suspected or confirmed influenza virus infections, encompassing seasonal, pandemic, and zoonotic influenza. Subgroups were pre-specified based on influenza type, age, and risk factors for poor outcomes, such as pregnancy, obesity, chronic health conditions, and immunosuppression. Critical outcomes of interest included mortality, hospital admission, duration of hospitalization, ICU admission, progression to mechanical ventilation, duration of symptoms, emergence of antiviral resistance, and adverse events related to therapeutic interventions. In 2023, evidence reviews were commissioned from four independent academic groups. Dr. Qiukui Hao and colleagues at McMaster University conducted a systematic review of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) on antivirals for severe influenza. They analyzed RCTs from major databases up to September 20, 2023, comparing direct-acting antivirals against placebo, standard care, or other antivirals. Dr. Hao's team also reviewed antivirals for non-severe influenza and prophylaxis against influenza, examining drugs such as baloxavir, favipiravir, laninamivir, oseltamivir, peramivir, umifenovir, and zanamivir. Dr. Barnaby Young and colleagues in Singapore updated a systematic review of adjunctive immunomodulatory therapies for severe influenza, originally conducted in 2019. As no specific RCTs on corticosteroids for severe influenza were identified, indirect evidence from other sources, including a 2023 systematic review of corticosteroids for community-acquired pneumonia and a Cochrane review of observational studies on corticosteroids in influenza, was analyzed. Ms. Shannon Kelly and colleagues at the University of Ottawa Heart Institute conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of antibiotic use in patients with non-confirmed symptomatic influenza at low risk of bacterial co-infection. Their search included studies from database inception to October 14, 2023. The GDG also reviewed influenza diagnostic testing strategies. Recognizing the lack of direct RCTs or observational studies comparing testing strategies, the GDG recommended a modeling approach. Yev Sahakkyan and Dr. Beate Sander from the Toronto Health Economics and Technology Assessment Collaborative developed a decision-analytic model to assess optimal testing strategies for patients with influenza-like illness. Six strategies were evaluated, ranging from no testing and no treatment to PCR testing with treatment decisions based on results. The GDG used the GRADE methodology to assess the quality of evidence and formulate recommendations. They considered the magnitude of benefits and harms, the quality of evidence, and stakeholder values and preferences. Strong recommendations were made when evidence was robust, while conditional recommendations were issued when evidence was less certain. The GDG avoided making strong recommendations based on low-quality evidence and documented discussions on feasibility, equity, and implementation considerations. Consensus was achieved on all recommendations without the need for formal voting. The GDG relied on their judgment to determine the minimally important difference (MID) for outcomes of interest, including the duration of symptoms in non-severe influenza. Equity implications, particularly for resource-limited settings, were also considered. The GDG aimed to provide actionable recommendations even in the face of uncertainty to support clinicians and patients while encouraging further research.
